name: Dermorphin

b.x: Seven amino acids from a tree frog's skin changed opioid pharmacology in 1981. Dermorphin (CAS 77614-16-5; H-Tyr-D-Ala-Phe-Gly-Tyr-Pro-Ser-NH2) binds mu-opioid receptors with a Kd of 0.46 nM in rat brain [6]. That makes it one of the most potent naturally occurring analgesics ever identified. Vittorio Erspamer's group isolated it from Phyllomedusa sauvagei skin and published its pharmacology in 1981 (Broccardo et al.) [1]. The mechanism is straightforward. A rare D-alanine at position 2 locks the peptide backbone into an ideal shape for mu-receptor activation and blocks enzymatic breakdown. In 1987, Kreil's group found a normal alanine codon at that spot in the precursor gene, which points to a conversion after translation [2]. When administered intrathecally to rodents, dermorphin proved 3,000 to 5,000 times more active than spinal morphine in standard pain assays [3]. In 1985, a double-blind randomized trial in 150 surgical patients compared intrathecal dermorphin with intrathecal morphine and intramuscular pentazocine [10]. Pain relief on dermorphin lasted about 43 hours, against 34 hours on morphine. Small IV studies in healthy volunteers ran from 1983 [11] to 1986 [12]. No later pain trial followed [5]. Dermorphin resurfaced in 2011, but not in a lab. It had been given to racehorses, unseen by standard equine drug screens, until tips from a few North American tracks surfaced that year [4]. In 2017 a federal jury convicted a Louisiana veterinarian and a Nebraska pharmacy of conspiring to sell it to improve race horse performance. ARCI now lists it as Class 1, its most serious tier. A 2018 review by Keppel Hesselink and Schatman [5] called for new intrathecal trials in postoperative pain and palliative care. No registered trial has followed. No modern clinical program exists. It isn't on the federal controlled substance schedules, and FDA has not approved it for humans or animals.

Dermorphin targets the mu-opioid receptor (MOR) with a binding affinity of approximately 0.46 nM, confirmed by equilibrium binding studies using tritiated dermorphin in rat brain membranes [6]. Selectivity is about 88-fold for mu over delta and more than 7,000-fold over kappa [6]. Once bound, dermorphin triggers Gi/Go protein coupling. Three downstream effects follow. Adenylyl cyclase gets inhibited, dropping intracellular cAMP. Voltage-gated N-type calcium channels close, cutting neurotransmitter release. Inwardly rectifying potassium channels (GIRKs) open, hyperpolarizing the neuron. Pain signal transmission shuts down at both spinal and supraspinal levels. The peptide's structure explains its potency. The N-terminal tetrapeptide Tyr-D-Ala-Phe-Gly is the "message" domain, responsible for receptor activation. The C-terminal tripeptide Tyr-Pro-Ser-NH2 is the "address" domain, directing selectivity toward mu-receptors specifically. Something interesting happens after binding. Dermorphin promotes MOR internalization through beta-arrestin recruitment. When researchers blocked this internalization in rats, the analgesic effect dropped [7]. Receptor trafficking isn't just a cleanup process; it actively contributes to pain relief. At the systems level, dermorphin modulates descending pain inhibitory pathways from the periaqueductal gray and rostral ventromedial medulla. It amplifies the body's own pain suppression circuits rather than working only at the site of injury.

Dermorphin benefits center on extreme analgesic potency and pharmacological selectivity, though most data comes from preclinical models, plus a 1985 intrathecal trial and small 1980s IV studies in volunteers.
Sub-microgram doses produce full analgesia in rodent models. Intrathecal administration showed 3,000-5,000x the potency of spinal morphine [3].

Mu-opioid receptor selectivity is about 88-fold over delta and more than 7,000-fold over kappa in rat brain binding [6]. That precision makes it a clean pharmacological tool for isolating mu-receptor signaling.
Tolerance develops more slowly than with morphine at equianalgesic doses in animal models. Naloxone-precipitated withdrawal also appears less intense in preclinical comparisons.
The D-Ala2 residue confers enzymatic resistance that endogenous opioid peptides lack. Activity duration extends well beyond what enkephalins or endorphins can achieve.
Dermorphin has served as a structural template for designing novel analgesic compounds. Glycodermorphin analogs showed improved blood-brain barrier penetration and prolonged activity [8].
A 1985 intrathecal trial in 150 surgical patients found pain relief lasted longer than with intrathecal morphine, about 43 versus 34 hours [10].

Potent mu-opioid agonist: 30-40x morphine in isolated-tissue assays, and 752-2,170x by intracerebroventricular injection in rats [1].

Dosing studied: No established human dose. Intrathecal RCT: a 20 mcg dose in surgical patients (PMID 3831962). Volunteer IV studies: 5.5 mcg/kg/min for 30 min (PMID 6833466). Equine study: 9.3 mcg/kg IV or IM (PMID 25376170).

A 1985 RCT in 150 surgical patients found intrathecal dermorphin outlasted intrathecal morphine and IM pentazocine [10]. Small IV studies in volunteers ran in 1983-1986; no later pain trial. No approved human use is known.
Key Study

Broccardo, Erspamer et al. 1981 (PMID 7195758): pharmacological characterization. Basso et al. 1985 (PMID 3831962): intrathecal RCT, 150 surgical patients. Robinson et al. 2015 (PMID 25376170): equine PK. Keppel Hesselink and Schatman 2018 (PMID 30538538): review.
Limitations

One clinical pain RCT (1985, 150 surgical patients, intrathecal); never replicated. No Phase 2/3 trials. The calculator dose tiers have no human source. Other human data are small 1983-1986 IV studies in volunteers on hormones and pain reflexes (PMID 6833466, PMID 3697765). One was placebo-controlled; no human PK study was found. No clinical development since the 1980s.

Community dosing: No community dosing data exists.
Community awareness is almost entirely limited to equine doping context. Extreme caution consensus among the few discussions that exist.

Science-Only Evidence

Science-only: published research exists (preclinical + 1 human RCT from 1985) but no community human-use protocols have emerged. The compound occupies a niche as an academic/pharmacological research tool, not a self-use peptide.
No established human dose

No human dose has been established for dermorphin, so this page shows no dose tiers. In a 1985 trial of 150 surgical patients, one group got a 20 mcg intrathecal dose for postoperative pain [10]. A 1986 study infused 0.16 mg/kg IV in healthy volunteers to test a pain reflex [12]. Neither one tested a subcutaneous dose.

Dermorphin is not a self-use peptide. It's listed as a research reference because its pharmacology is genuinely interesting, but the risk profile makes it wholly inappropriate for self-administration. No human dose has been established. A 1985 trial of 150 surgical patients gave one group 20 mcg intrathecally for postoperative pain [10]. A 1986 study infused 0.16 mg/kg IV in healthy volunteers to test a pain reflex, not to treat pain [12]. Neither one tested a subcutaneous dose. Reconstitution math only: a 1 mg vial with 2 mL bacteriostatic water gives 500 mcg/mL. Each unit on a U-100 insulin syringe then holds 5 mcg. A 2 mg vial with the same 2 mL gives 1,000 mcg/mL, or 10 mcg per unit. The thing most people miss: plasma half-life (~1.3 min in rodents, ~5.4 min in horses) does not equal duration of action. Receptor binding and beta-arrestin-mediated internalization sustain the analgesic effect for 45-90 minutes IV, and up to 48 hours intrathecally. Don't confuse clearance from blood with clearance from the receptor. Naloxone on hand is non-negotiable. Analytical-grade sourcing with LC-MS/MS purity verification is also non-negotiable.
Cycling

DEPENDENCE WARNING: Dermorphin should not be used in repeated dosing protocols outside of strictly controlled research settings. Even short-duration repeated exposure carries risk of physical dependence and opioid withdrawal. There is no established or recommended cycling protocol for human use. Any investigational protocol must include naloxone availability and medical supervision. Tolerance to analgesic effects can develop within days of repeated administration.
Dermorphin Cycle

Repeated mu-opioid receptor activation leads to beta-arrestin-mediated receptor internalization, desensitization, and downregulation. Analgesic tolerance develops within days. Physical dependence compounds cycling risk: off-periods carry opioid withdrawal risk. The 1-on/4-off cycling structure on this page is a harm-reduction framework, NOT a recommended use protocol. In practice, no cycling protocol is appropriate outside strictly controlled research.
Reduced analgesic response at same dose (tolerance onset)
Dose escalation urge: escalating to maintain effect is a dependence indicator
Restlessness, anxiety, or irritability during off periods (early withdrawal)
Insomnia, muscle aches, or GI disturbance when compound is withheld

Continuous pulse oximetry and respiratory rate monitoring required for at least 60 minutes post-administration. SpO2 must stay at or above 95%. Respiratory rate must stay at or above 12 breaths per minute.

Store reconstituted solution at 2-8 degrees C and use within 7 days. For IV research applications, use within 24 hours. Lyophilized powder stores up to 24 months at -20 degrees C, desiccated, protected from light.
Handle it as if it were a controlled substance, even though it is unscheduled: locked storage, usage logs, and proper waste disposal.

Works With
Avoid
Benzodiazepines (diazepam, clonazepam, alprazolam)
Severe additive CNS and respiratory depression; combination is potentially fatal. Black box warning equivalent.
Other opioid agonists (morphine, fentanyl, oxycodone, tramadol)
Additive mu-opioid receptor activation; compounded respiratory depression and overdose risk.

MAO inhibitors (phenelzine, selegiline, tranylcypromine)
Risk of serotonin syndrome and unpredictable potentiation of opioid effects. Contraindicated.

Respiratory depression can kill you. That is the primary risk with dermorphin, and its 30-40x morphine potency makes the margin for error vanishingly small. Bolus injection induced apnea in animal models. In any setting where this peptide is handled, naloxone (0.4-2 mg IV) must be within arm's reach. The full spectrum of mu-opioid agonist effects applies. Profound sedation. Nausea and vomiting. Constipation and reduced gastrointestinal motility. Miosis. Bradycardia. Urinary retention. These are well-characterized opioid effects, but dermorphin's extreme potency compresses the dose-response curve. Small dosing errors produce disproportionate consequences. Human safety data is almost nonexistent. One 1985 intrathecal trial and no modern pharmacovigilance data. Everything known about dermorphin's side effect profile comes from preclinical animal models and equine pharmacokinetic studies. That's roughly 250 PubMed publications total, with no controlled human dose-finding work. Physical dependence develops with repeated administration. Preclinical data suggest withdrawal may be less intense than morphine withdrawal at equianalgesic doses, but "less intense opioid withdrawal" is still opioid withdrawal. Symptoms include agitation, muscle pain, insomnia, diarrhea, and autonomic instability. Dependence signs can emerge within days of repeated dosing. Addiction potential is high. Dermorphin is a potent mu-opioid agonist. Mu-receptor activation drives the reward pathway. Anyone with a history of substance use disorder faces extreme risk. Tolerance to the analgesic effect develops with chronic use, driving dose escalation. Drug interactions compound every risk listed above. Benzodiazepines combined with dermorphin create severe additive CNS and respiratory depression; that combination can be fatal. The same applies to other opioid agonists, alcohol, barbiturates, and general anesthetics. MAO inhibitors create risk of serotonin syndrome and unpredictable opioid potentiation. Gabapentinoids (gabapentin, pregabalin) carry an FDA warning for increased respiratory depression when combined with opioids. Contraindications are extensive. Pregnancy and breastfeeding (opioid peptides cross the placental barrier). Respiratory insufficiency or sleep apnea. Severe hepatic impairment. Concurrent MAO inhibitor use. Paralytic ileus. Traumatic brain injury with raised intracranial pressure. Unmonitored settings without naloxone access. Pediatric populations have zero safety data. Stop immediately and seek emergency care if respiratory rate drops below 12 breaths per minute, SpO2 falls below 95%, or any signs of opioid toxicity appear.
Common Issues & Solutions
No reversal agent present: unacceptable in any research setting: naloxone 0.4–2 mg IV must be immediately accessible before any dermorphin handling.
Confusing plasma half-life (~1.3–5.4 min) with duration of action: receptor binding and internalization extend analgesic effect 45–90 min IV, up to 48 h intrathecal: far beyond plasma clearance.

Assuming "research-only" label = legal to possess: dermorphin isn't federally scheduled, but FDA has not approved it for humans or animals. Selling it for race horses led to 2017 federal convictions; legal risk is substantial.

Repeated dosing producing tolerance/withdrawal: physical dependence can emerge within days; even short repeated-dosing research protocols require dependence monitoring and withdrawal management planning.
Contamination risk: uncertified research-grade dermorphin may contain incorrect peptide, degradation products, or microbial contaminants; LC-MS/MS purity verification is essential.

Dermorphin is not listed in the US Controlled Substances Act schedules (21 CFR 1308) or on the DEA's controlled substance list. The Federal Analogue Act (21 U.S.C. 813) can treat an unlisted drug as Schedule I. It applies when the drug is meant for human consumption and is an analogue of a Schedule I or II drug. The statute pairs a chemical-structure test with an effect test; in McFadden v. United States (2015) the government accepted, and the Supreme Court assumed, that both must be shown. No DEA statement or court ruling applying it to dermorphin was found. The Association of Racing Commissioners International (ARCI) lists dermorphin as Class 1, Penalty Class A, its most serious tier for horse racing. In 2017, a federal jury in Louisiana convicted a veterinarian and a Nebraska pharmacy of conspiring to sell it for race horses. The jury also convicted on adulterated or misbranded drug counts under the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, not a controlled substance charge. The Justice Department noted FDA has not approved it for humans or animals. WADA's 2026 Prohibited List does not name dermorphin, and its S7 narcotics section is a closed list. Its S0 section bans, at all times, any substance with no current approval for human therapeutic use, and none is known for dermorphin. Rules outside the US vary, and no foreign listing was confirmed for this page. Researchers should verify local regulations before procurement, possession, or use. This content is provided for educational and research reference only. No regulator is known to have approved dermorphin for human therapeutic use. Nothing on this page constitutes medical advice or encouragement to obtain, possess, or self-administer this compound.

faqs.q: Why is dermorphin listed as "research-only" when it is an unapproved opioid?
faqs.a: Dermorphin isn't listed in the US Controlled Substances Act schedules (21 CFR 1308). The Federal Analogue Act (21 U.S.C. § 813) reaches unlisted drugs meant for human consumption that are analogues of Schedule I or II drugs. The statute pairs a chemical-structure test with an effect test; in McFadden v. United States (2015) the government accepted, and the Supreme Court assumed, that both must be shown. No DEA statement or court ruling applying it to dermorphin was found. A 2017 federal horse-doping case in Louisiana ended in conspiracy and adulterated or misbranded drug convictions, not a controlled substance charge.

faqs.q: What happened with the horse racing doping scandal?
faqs.a: Dermorphin went undetected in horse racing until 2011. Tips from a few North American tracks then pointed to it, and labs built new tests (PMID 23571464). In 2017 a federal jury convicted a Louisiana veterinarian and a Nebraska pharmacy of conspiring to sell it to improve the performance of race horses. ARCI lists it as Class 1, Penalty Class A, its most serious tier.

faqs.q: Was there ever a human clinical trial with dermorphin?
faqs.a: Yes. A 1985 double-blind randomized trial in 150 surgical patients compared intrathecal dermorphin with intrathecal morphine and intramuscular pentazocine (PMID 3831962). Dermorphin pain relief lasted longest, about 43 hours. Small IV studies in healthy volunteers ran from 1983 to 1986 (PMID 6833466). No pain trial has followed since (PMID 30538538).

faqs.q: Why does the analgesic effect last so long despite the short plasma half-life?
faqs.a: Plasma half-life (distribution phase) is very short (~1.3 min rodent / ~5.4 min equine), meaning dermorphin clears from plasma rapidly. But receptor binding at mu-opioid receptors and subsequent receptor internalization via beta-arrestin recruitment sustains the analgesic effect well beyond plasma availability. In the 1985 surgical trial, one intrathecal dose gave pain relief lasting about 43 hours on average (PMID 3831962).

faqs.q: Could dermorphin ever become a clinical drug for cancer pain?
faqs.a: Theoretically, its extreme potency, mu-selectivity, and potentially slower tolerance development are interesting for palliative care (see PMID 30538538). Practically, regulatory, addiction-liability, and commercial hurdles are enormous. No pharmaceutical company has advanced dermorphin into modern clinical development.

summary: Thirty to forty times more potent than morphine, and it comes from a frog. Dermorphin (H-Tyr-D-Ala-Phe-Gly-Tyr-Pro-Ser-NH2) is a seven-amino-acid opioid peptide first isolated in 1981 from the skin of South American tree frogs in the genus Phyllomedusa.
